title: Topologies & Network Types
summary: How devices are wired together and what scale that network covers — from the cable in your room to the internet itself.

blocks.markdown:
A **topology** is the arrangement — physical or logical — of how devices connect in a network.

- It shapes **cost**, **fault tolerance**, and **performance**.
- Five shapes cover almost all real networks: bus, star, ring, mesh, hybrid.
- Separately, networks are classed by **scale**: PAN, LAN, MAN, WAN.
- The internet is a **network of networks** — millions of LANs and WANs linked together.

A topology answers: **which devices connect to which, and how?**

- **Physical topology** — the actual cables or wireless links.
- **Logical topology** — how data flows, which may differ from physical wiring.

Choosing a topology is an early design decision: it determines how many cables you need, where failures bite, and how easy expansion is. See [network-fundamentals](network-fundamentals) for signal basics.

blocks.subTitle: Bus
blocks.markdown:
**Bus topology** — all devices share one cable (the bus). A signal travels the full length; every device sees it but only the addressed one responds.

- **Pro:** cheap, simple — one cable.
- **Con:** one cable break kills the whole network; performance drops as more devices share the bus.

Used in early Ethernet; rare in modern wired networks.

blocks.subTitle: Star
blocks.markdown:
**Star topology** — every device connects to a central **switch** or **hub**; no direct device-to-device cable.

- **Pro:** one device fails without affecting others; easy to add/remove nodes.
- **Con:** central switch is a **single point of failure** — if it fails, the whole network goes down.

The most common topology in office LANs today.

blocks.subTitle: Ring
blocks.markdown:
**Ring topology** — devices form a closed loop; data travels in one direction (or both in dual-ring) passing each node.

- **Pro:** predictable, equal access; no collisions.
- **Con:** a single break in the ring stops the whole network (in single-ring); slower setup.

Used in SONET/SDH fiber rings for telcos.

blocks.subTitle: Mesh & Hybrid
blocks.markdown:
**Mesh topology** — every device connects to every other. **Full mesh** = N×(N−1)/2 links. **Partial mesh** = only critical nodes are fully connected.

- **Pro:** multiple paths — one link failure doesn't break connectivity.
- **Con:** expensive; many cables and ports.

**Hybrid** combines two or more topologies, e.g. a star-bus or star-ring. Most real enterprise networks are hybrids.

blocks.subTitle: Pros & cons at a glance
blocks.markdown:
| Topology | Strength | Weakness |
|---|---|---|
| Bus | Cheapest | One break = full outage |
| Star | Easy to manage | Central switch is SPOF |
| Ring | Orderly access | Break disrupts loop |
| Mesh | High resilience | Costly, complex cabling |
| Hybrid | Flexible | Design complexity |

Networks are also classified by the **geographic area** they cover.

| Type | Full name | Typical range |
|---|---|---|
| PAN | Personal Area Network | ~10 m (body/desk) |
| LAN | Local Area Network | Building / campus |
| MAN | Metropolitan Area Network | City / region |
| WAN | Wide Area Network | Country / globe |

**PAN** example: Bluetooth between phone and headphones. **LAN** example: office Wi-Fi. **WAN** example: leased lines connecting branch offices across countries.

**Wired** (Ethernet, fiber) — signal travels over copper or glass.

- **Pro:** high speed, low latency, more secure (no air interface).
- **Con:** cables limit mobility; installation cost.

**Wireless** (Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, cellular) — signal travels through air.

- **Pro:** mobility, no cable runs.
- **Con:** shared medium → interference; range limits; security needs extra care.

Most real networks combine both — wired backbone, wireless at the edge.

The **internet** is not a single network — it is a **network of networks**.

- Thousands of **ISPs** (Internet Service Providers) each run their own WAN or LAN.
- They connect at **IXPs** (Internet Exchange Points) where traffic crosses between providers.
- **BGP** (Border Gateway Protocol) is the routing protocol that glues them — routers announce which address ranges they can reach.

So when you load a webpage, packets may cross several independent networks before arriving. See [network-devices](network-devices) for the hardware involved.

blocks.subTitle: Star vs mesh trade-offs
blocks.markdown:
⭐ **Q: Star vs mesh — when would you choose each?**

**Star** when cost and simplicity matter most and a reliable central switch is acceptable. **Mesh** when resilience is critical (data centres, backbone links) and you can afford the extra hardware. Partial mesh is the practical middle ground — only high-priority nodes are fully interconnected.

blocks.subTitle: LAN vs MAN vs WAN
blocks.markdown:
⭐ **Q: What is the difference between LAN, MAN, and WAN?**

**LAN** covers a building or campus — high speed, privately owned. **MAN** covers a city — often a carrier-managed fiber ring. **WAN** spans countries or the globe — uses leased lines, MPLS, or the internet. The key axis is **scale**, which drives cost and ownership model.

blocks.subTitle: Why star dominates LANs
blocks.markdown:
**Q: Why is star the most common LAN topology today?**

Because Ethernet switches are cheap and a single-switch failure only takes down the network — not individual cables. Every device gets its own dedicated link, so one host's problem doesn't slow others. Troubleshooting is also simple: swap the cable or the port.

Bus had collisions that got worse at scale; star avoids them entirely.
